scope.description: Focused hand-researched deepening pass for English Base Set, beginning with Alakazam #1 as a launch-holo, Japanese Expansion Pack lineage, artist-credit, play-memory, and print-boundary test case.

Pokemon TCG API v2 card record: Alakazam base1-1
Pokemon TCG API v2 set record: Base Set
Local Japanese pre-English catalog: Alakazam / PMCG1-049

claims.text: The local English WoC catalog and Pokemon TCG API identify base1-1 as Alakazam, Base Set card 1/102, Rare Holo.
The local row and Bulbapedia model this Alakazam as a Stage 2 Psychic Pokemon, Level 42, 80 HP, evolving from Kadabra, with Psychic weakness and three-Colorless retreat cost.

The card's Pokemon Power is Damage Swap, which moves damage counters among the player's Pokemon without knocking one out, and its attack is Confuse Ray for 30 damage with a coin-flip chance to Confuse.

The local English row, Pokemon TCG API, and Bulbapedia credit Alakazam base1-1 to Ken Sugimori; the related Japanese pre-English row carries a local illustrator crosswalk to Ken Sugimori but does not itself become direct Japanese-print authority.

Bulbapedia and the local catalog place English Base Set on January 9, 1999, with Japanese Expansion Pack lineage from October 20, 1996; Bulbapedia describes Base Set as the first main English expansion and tied to Red/Blue and Red/Green launch-era Pokemon.
Bulbapedia lists Alakazam as first released in Japanese Expansion Pack, and the local Japanese pre-English catalog carries the related Alakazam row as PMCG1-049 / Holo Rare / active No Rarity target.

Base Set Alakazam #1/102 must be kept separate from Japanese Expansion Pack / No Rarity PMCG1-049, Base Set 2 #1/130, Legendary Collection #1/110, Game Boy records, and English print states such as First Edition, Shadowless, Unlimited, and 4th print.

Bulbapedia describes early English Base Set print differences such as First Edition, Shadowless, thinner text, missing artwork-window shadows, and a later 1999-2000 copyright line, but a catalog row alone does not identify which print state a seller's card occupies.

Bulbapedia ties the English Pokedex text to Red/Blue and the Japanese text to Red/Green; the English entry leans on Alakazam's supercomputer-level brain and IQ lore, while the Japanese entry emphasizes extrasensory power over physical attacks.

Bulbapedia notes that Confuse Ray is a move in the Pokemon games that Alakazam cannot learn, making this card a small reminder that early TCG mechanics and video-game movepools were related but not identical systems.

Alakazam opens English Base Set's holo numbering with a control-engine idea instead of brute force: Damage Swap made the board feel rearrangeable, while Sugimori's calm psychic pose made the first card in the set feel like a mind holding the table together.

steps: Preserve release_family_id en_wotc_base_set_19990109, local row id base1-1, printed number 1/102, Rare Holo, Ken Sugimori credit, Damage Swap, and Confuse Ray.
Do not infer First Edition, Shadowless, Unlimited, 4th print, copyright-line state, condition, price, or authenticity from the catalog row or reference image.
Do not collapse the English Base Set row into Japanese Expansion Pack / No Rarity PMCG1-049; No Rarity requires its own Japanese-card visual evidence and human or verifier confirmation.
Do not collapse the row into Base Set 2 #1/130, Legendary Collection #1/110, or Game Boy records even when the name, art, or attack memory overlaps.

card_highlights.rarity_signal: Rare Holo; Base Set #1/102, separate from Japanese Expansion Pack / No Rarity PMCG1-049, Base Set 2 #1/130, Legendary Collection #1/110, and English print-run states.
card_highlights.collector_texture_note: Base Set starts at #1 with Alakazam, not Charizard. That makes the binder opening feel quieter and stranger: the first holo is the psychic one that moves damage around and asks the table to think.

narrative.human_title: The brain at the front of Base Set
narrative.why_it_matters: Alakazam is a beautiful first row because it does not win by roaring. It sits at the front of English Base Set as a holo mind: Ken Sugimori's psychic silhouette, Damage Swap bending the whole board, Confuse Ray carrying early TCG weirdness, and a Japanese Expansion Pack ancestor sitting behind it. For a collector agent, this card is also a boundary lesson. Same name and similar memory can point toward No Rarity, Shadowless, Base Set 2, Legendary Collection, or a Game Boy record. None of those are granted by resemblance. The row tells you where to look; the seller evidence has to tell you what is actually in hand.

claims.text: The local English WoC catalog and Pokemon TCG API identify base1-11 as Nidoking, Base Set card 11/102, Rare Holo.
The local row models this Nidoking as a Stage 2 Grass-type Pokemon, Level 23, 90 HP, evolving from Nidorino, with Psychic weakness and a three-Colorless retreat cost.

The card's attacks are Thrash, a 30+ damage coin-flip attack that can recoil 10 damage onto Nidoking, and Toxic, which poisons the Defending Pokemon for 20 poison damage instead of 10 after each player's turn.

The local English row and Pokemon TCG API credit Nidoking base1-11 to Ken Sugimori; the related Japanese pre-English row carries the same local illustrator crosswalk but does not itself become direct Japanese-print authority.

The local Japanese pre-English catalog carries the related Nidoking row as PMCG1-013 / Holo Rare / active No Rarity target, giving the English Base Set row a Japanese Expansion Pack lineage lane without proving any seller's card is No Rarity.
The local catalog and Pokemon TCG API place Nidoking inside English Base Set, the 102-card Wizards release dated January 9, 1999.

Base Set Nidoking #11/102 must be kept separate from Japanese Expansion Pack / No Rarity PMCG1-013, Base Set 2 reprint memory, and English print states such as First Edition, Shadowless, Unlimited, and 4th print.

Nidoking is one of Base Set's early holo bruisers: the row carries monster-weight, poison pressure, recoil risk, and Sugimori's kaiju-like silhouette, making it a different kind of launch memory from Charizard's celebrity or Alakazam's control puzzle.

card_highlights.rarity_signal: Rare Holo; Base Set #11/102, separate from Japanese Expansion Pack / No Rarity PMCG1-013 and English print-run states.
card_highlights.collector_texture_note: Nidoking feels like old Pokemon cardboard getting loud: spines, weight, poison, recoil, and a holo surface that makes the boss monster feel physically present.

narrative.human_title: The launch holo with boss weight
narrative.why_it_matters: Nidoking is not subtle, and that is the point. In Base Set it gives the holo lineup a heavy, spiked, poisonous body: Thrash can hurt itself, Toxic makes poison feel nastier than usual, and Sugimori's posture turns a Stage 2 Grass row into something closer to a kaiju stamp. The Japanese Expansion Pack ancestor, PMCG1-013, makes it especially useful for agents because the same creature memory can pull toward English Base Set, Japanese No Rarity, or later reprint talk. The card is a thrill, but the catalog lesson is strict: monster recognition is not provenance.

claims.text: The local English WoC catalog and Pokemon TCG API identify base1-12 as Ninetales, Base Set card 12/102, Rare Holo.
The local row models this Ninetales as a Stage 1 Fire Pokemon, Level 32, 80 HP, evolving from Vulpix, with Water weakness and a one-Colorless retreat cost.
The card's attacks are Lure, which pulls an opposing Benched Pokemon into the Active spot, and Fire Blast, an 80-damage attack that discards a Fire Energy attached to Ninetales.

The local English row and Pokemon TCG API credit Ninetales base1-12 to Ken Sugimori; the related Japanese pre-English row carries the same local illustrator crosswalk but does not itself become direct Japanese-print authority.

The local Japanese pre-English catalog carries the related Ninetales row as PMCG1-022 / Holo Rare / active No Rarity target, giving the English Base Set row a Japanese Expansion Pack lineage lane without proving any seller's card is No Rarity.
The local catalog and Pokemon TCG API place Ninetales inside English Base Set, the 102-card Wizards release dated January 9, 1999.

Base Set Ninetales #12/102 must be kept separate from Japanese Expansion Pack / No Rarity PMCG1-022, Base Set 2 reprint memory, and English print states such as First Edition, Shadowless, Unlimited, and 4th print.

Ninetales is one of Base Set's most atmospheric holos: a graceful Fire Stage 1 whose Lure and Fire Blast text pairs elegance with danger, while the holo surface makes condition and surface evidence especially important to collectors.

card_highlights.collector_texture_note: Ninetales is the quiet fire in Base Set: elegant, dangerous, and absolutely dependent on the holo surface telling the truth. Scratches in that firelight matter.

narrative.why_it_matters: Ninetales is where Base Set stops feeling only like monsters and starts feeling like atmosphere. It evolves from Vulpix into something graceful, a Fire holo that can pull a target forward with Lure and then spend four Fire Energy on a huge Fire Blast. Sugimori's art gives it poise instead of noise, which is why condition matters so much: the holo is part of the feeling, not just a rarity marker. The Japanese Expansion Pack ancestor, PMCG1-022, also makes it a clean agent lesson. A Ninetales memory can be English Base Set, Japanese No Rarity, Base Set 2, or a print-state question. Beauty is not provenance; the scan has to speak.
